A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable through their appendices and describe the same Meditron/L+M-24 research. Retained experiments, equations, and illustrations can be matched despite substantial rewriting, retitling, and a new evaluation contribution.

before.justification: V1 reports original alignment and model-fusion experiments, translation scores on 3k unseen pairs, hallucination analyses, and training-efficiency results.

after.justification: V2 retains the original translation experiments and adds atomic-level NLI evaluation results, evaluator comparisons, and diagnostic caption cases.

M1.justification: V2 introduces an atomic-level evaluation algorithm: an LLM decomposes captions, an NLI model assesses every atomic pairing, and pooling produces hallucination and coverage scores. This substantially replaces v1's evaluation approach. The underlying Meditron alignment and TIES/SLERP translation pipeline is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same documented L+M-24 domain coverage and supplementary unseen-pair scenario. Molecule generation and caption generation remain evaluated in both directions, despite v2's caption-focused title. Atomic scoring changes evaluation procedures, not the represented datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds a substantive evaluator comparison against full NLI, SummaC Conv, and SummaC ZS in Figure 5. The comparator membership in the four retained translation-result tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 replaces the aggregate length, Chr-F, and win-rate evaluation with atomic hallucination/coverage scoring and KL comparisons of coverage distributions. The latter labels CPO+SLERP outputs preferred and Meditron outputs dispreferred. Reported training proportions, sample counts, backbone, merging ratio, and training configuration remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 replaces v1's aggregate win-rate analysis and main-text memorisation case study with NLI-granularity diagnostics and five cases examining missing or unsupported caption content (Figure 5 and Table 6). The original appendix generation examples and training-convergence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both display descriptive score distributions; the added NLI probabilities and KL scores serve as evaluation measures rather than experimental uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V1 Tables 1–4 match v2 Tables 2–5 numerically. V2 newly reports atomic coverage of 0.69 for SLERP+CPO versus 0.51 for Meditron, and evaluator KL scores of 0.54 versus 0.12–0.17 (Figures 4–5). V1's aggregate length, Chr-F, entailment, and win-rate results are removed. These are changed evaluation results, not same-metric translation improvements.

T1.justification: V2 introduces formal definitions of atomic hallucination and coverage using minimum contradiction and maximum entailment pooling (Equations 6–7). RLHF and HALO mathematics is retained in Appendix A. The compressed CPO and KTO expressions in Table 1 also introduce sign inconsistencies relative to v1's objectives; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

C1.justification: The contributions shift from first applications of human-centric optimisation and nonlinear fusion for bidirectional translation, plus domain-agnostic hallucination checks, toward minimal-training merging/alignment synergies and claimed superiority of atomic NLI for caption evaluation. The central efficiency and strong translation-performance claims persist.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the caption advantage chiefly as improved coverage while all models show low hallucination, and adds a structured-learning/generalisation explanation for CPO. Its new limitations discuss static merging, atomic over-fragmentation, evaluator-model dependence, valid unsupported content, and uncertain transfer beyond chemistry, substantially extending v1's brief qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses TIES's 20% parameter retention, the 635k-pair sampling pool, the atomic-decomposition prompt, Meta-Llama-3-8B, and the specific DeBERTa checkpoint. Existing translation prompts, QLoRA settings, and the 19:1 merging ratio are retained. These disclosures do not establish changes to the earlier experiments.

R1.justification: The chemistry-focused related-work appendix becomes a substantially expanded Section 2 covering chemistry, model merging, alignment, and NLI evaluation. New literature, including Ilharco, Laban, Schuster, and Yang, supports detailed positioning against merging families and different NLI granularities.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, methodology, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves into the main text, RLHF foundations move to Appendix A, merging precedes alignment in the method narrative, and optimisation explanations are compressed into a table.

P2.justification: V2 changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, adds pipeline and method diagrams (Figures 1–3), replaces evaluation graphics, and adds an objective table and diagnostic case table. Existing result tables, prompts, generation examples, and training plots are reformatted or relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 improves exposition, implementation disclosure, and limitations, and separates caption coverage from factuality. However, its rewritten CPO/KTO formulas introduce sign inconsistencies, and evaluator superiority is assessed using preferences assigned by generating model without independent quality labels (Section 4.2.3). Table 6 also assigns 0.02 hallucination to antiviral/HCV assertions absent from the reference. With translation results unchanged, these benefits and correctness concerns prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
